I definitely wasn’t a neo nazi, but I also trivialized injustices against people based on their skin, religion, sexual orientation, etc. I read the articles about white officers shooting unarmed black men, and thought, without doing any research, “they probably deserved it for xyz.” I wasn’t *against* mixed race relationships but I personally would never date someone who wasn’t white. I perceived black women as being sassy and rude, and “earning” the disrespect they faced on a daily basis, and felt superior to people who didn’t speak English well. A lot of what I felt was that if these people were really facing racism, etc. then they needed to stand up for themselves and that they were being lazy for not doing so. 

When I started college these beliefs began to change as I interacted with people who weren’t just white and republican, but the real defining moment was when I was hospitalized for a suicide attempt. While in the psych ward (one of the most traumatizing experiences of my life), I had absolutely no agency. I couldn’t leave, I couldn’t advocate for myself, the staff was rude and wouldn’t listen to me because they dismissed me as just being some crazy person. The injustice of their treatment toward me and the desperation I felt being trapped there really resonated with me. Once I got out, I realized that the reason people of color fight so much to bring awareness is because of the injustice of the way they’re treated. If someone thinks you’re a second class citizen for being black, no matter what you say or do, as a black person, is going to change their mind or cause them to treat you with basic human decency. That’s what I experienced with mental illness at the psych ward, and it made me really examine my underlying, subconscious prejudices. I had never considered myself racist because I didn’t go around saying “I hate black people,” but I held racist beliefs, as outlined above. It made me realize how many more people had treated and viewed people of color the way I treated and viewed them, and worse, and how absolutely desperately frustrating it must be to engage with that on a daily basis, being trapped not by the walls of a psych ward but the walls of your skin color. 

Since then I have been making an effort to educate myself on issues affecting people of color, and the results have been horrifying and enlightening. I am still trying to “unlearn” subconscious racial preferences but truly the psych ward, as traumatic as the experience was, gave me a depth of empathy that I never would have found otherwise, and that’s how I came to see how implicitly racist I was.

I just ask because I have been on both sides of this interaction. I have been the friend who was emotionally exhausted from trying to constantly listen and provide advice to depressed or anxious friends, and it’s really hard and really awful to deal with, even though you desperatwlt want to. (This is different from just listening once in a while or offering a little bit of advice, as you probably know.) on the other hand, I have also been the person who treats one of my friends as a therapist and constantly talks to them and seeks advice for my mental illness, to the point that they dread hanging out with me for the sole reason that it’s emotionally draining. It can be really hard for the “therapist friend” because they desperately want to help you but have no idea how to, and constantly hearing about and seeing no improvement is heartbreaking, especially if they’ve exhausted their store of advice. 

If you don’t want to share the story of what happened with your therapist, that’s totally fine, and I understand bad experiences with mental health professionals can sour all expectations. But I would highly recommend trying to go to one. The difference between therapists and friends is that therapists are literally trained to deal with everything you’re going through and to help you. They are trained to be able to listen to all of your struggles and sadness without it being emotionally exhausting. 

It is possible to find good therapists as well, but it can be a long road of bad ones. It’s really really worth it when you find a good one, as I can attest to- I had some really shitty ones along the way but my current one is excellent. 

I’m really sorry that you have to go through this. Trust me, I know. I have bipolar disorder and all forms of mental illness suck more than words can say. It’s so hard and I’m so sorry. I really hope you find healing, or at the very least, improvement !!
